q: How do you say the c in ciao?
why: c before i or e sounds like ch, and the i in cia is not said.

q: What does the double t in notte tell you?
o: Say the t twice, with a vowel between
Nothing: it sounds like one t
Hold the t a little longer
Make the o before it long
why: A double consonant is held longer, and it changes the word: notte, night.

q: How do you say the sch in bruschetta?
why: sch is always a hard sk sound in Italian.

q: You check in at a hotel in the morning. What do you say to the receptionist?
why: A stranger at work gets a polite greeting and the Lei form: Buongiorno, come sta?

q: Why is it buonasera but buongiorno?
o: sera is feminine and giorno is masculine, and the word for good changes to match
why: buono agrees with the noun: giorno is masculine, sera is feminine.

q: How is the formal you written?
why: Lei with a capital L is the formal you; lei with a small l means she.

q: Which is right?
why: problema ends in -a but is masculine: il problema.

q: What is the plural of la chiave (the key)?
why: -e becomes -i in the plural, and la becomes le: le chiavi.

q: How can you tell the gender of a noun ending in -e, like pane?
o: Learn it with its article: the ending gives no clue
It is the same as in English
why: Nouns in -e can be either gender: il pane, la chiave.

q: Which article goes with zaino (backpack), a masculine noun that starts with z?
why: Masculine nouns starting with z take lo: lo zaino.

q: How do you say the friends (a group of men)?
why: amici is masculine plural and starts with a vowel: gli amici.

q: How do you say I like coffee?
why: Things in general take the article in Italian: il caffè.

q: What does Lei with a capital L mean?
why: Lei with a capital L is the formal you; lei with a small l is she.

q: How do you ask two friends how they are?
why: voi, for more than one person, takes state.

q: Why is Sto bene enough, without io?
o: The ending of sto already shows that the subject is I
why: The verb ending tells you who: sto can only mean I am.

q: How do you say I'm hungry?
why: Hunger uses avere: ho fame, literally I have hunger.

q: What is the difference between è and e?
o: è means is; e means and
è means and; e means is
why: The accent makes è the verb: Luca è stanco. Without it, e means and.

q: Which form of essere goes with voi?
why: voi takes siete: Siete americani?

q: Where does a color go?
o: Before the noun, as in English
At the end of the sentence
why: Colors go after the noun: la camicia bianca.

q: the white shirts =
why: Feminine plural noun, feminine plural adjective, after the noun: le camicie bianche.

q: Which adjective has the same form with il and la?
why: Adjectives in -e do not change for gender: il cappotto verde, la borsa verde.

q: Which form goes with Lei (formal you)?
why: Lei takes the lui / lei form: parla.

q: Lavoro in un ufficio can mean…
o: I work, or I'm working, in an office
Only I worked in an office
why: The Italian present covers both I work and I'm working, and the -o ending means I.

q: What is the loro form of capire?
why: capire is an -isc- verb: capiscono.

q: How do you turn Parli italiano (you speak Italian) into a question?
o: Put che in front of it
Keep the words and raise your voice at the end
Move the verb to the end
Put the subject after the verb and add non
why: Italian has no helper verb: the same words with a rising voice make the question.

q: How many sisters do you have? =
why: quanto agrees with its noun: sorelle is feminine plural, so quante.

q: Which spelling is right?
why: qual è is written with no apostrophe.

q: There are two banks downtown. =
why: More than one thing takes ci sono.

q: Your friend knows which pharmacy you mean. How do you say it's downtown?
why: A particular place you name with la: è says where it is.

q: What does È un bar mean?
why: Without ci, è just means it is.

q: It's five o'clock. =
why: Hours from two on are feminine plural: sono le cinque.

q: Which is right for twenty-eight?
why: venti drops its i before otto, and it is all one word: ventotto.

q: How do you say ten euros?
why: euro never changes: un euro, dieci euro.

q: Giulia is Marco's sister. How does Marco's friend say his sister?
why: sua agrees with sorella, not with Marco, and one family member takes no article.

q: Which is right?
why: With a singular family word, no article: mia madre.

q: What does la sua casa mean?
why: sua agrees with casa, so it can mean his or her.

q: I'm going to the bank. =
why: Many everyday places take in with no article: in banca.

q: di + il =
why: di and il join into del.

q: What does Sono di Milano mean?
why: di with a city says where you are from.

q: It's hot today. =
why: Weather uses fare: fa caldo.

q: Your friend calls you from the kitchen. You answer I'm coming! =
why: Moving toward the person you talk to takes venire: vengo.

q: Which is the loro form of andare?
why: andare is irregular: the loro form is vanno.

q: You need help from a stranger on the street. You say:
why: With a stranger, use the Lei form of potere: può.

q: The polite way to ask a pharmacist for something starts with:
why: vorrei means I would like: the polite way to ask.

q: Luisa can play the piano (she learned how). =
why: A learned skill takes sapere: sa suonare.

q: I like the shoes. =
why: le scarpe is plural, so piacciono agrees with it, and the article stays.

q: Mi piace il gelato. How do you say Me too?
why: With piacere, me too is anche a me.

q: Do you like music? (to a stranger) =
why: For a stranger, Le, and la musica is one thing: piace.

q: "My name is Emma" is…
why: chiamarsi is reflexive: mi chiamo. Chiamo Emma means I'm calling Emma.

q: "We get up at seven" is…
why: With noi, both parts match: ci and the -iamo ending.

q: "I have to get up at six" is…
why: The pronoun joins the infinitive and matches io: alzarmi. Mi devo alzare is also right.

q: "La borsa? ___ prendo." Which word fits?
why: borsa is feminine and singular, so la.

q: "The shoes? I'll take them." is…
why: scarpe is feminine plural, so le, and it goes before the verb.

q: "Can I try it on?" (il maglione) is…
why: maglione is masculine, so lo, joined to the infinitive. Lo posso provare? is also right.

q: Which is the polite way to order a coffee?
why: vorrei (I would like) is polite; voglio sounds like a demand.

q: "Don't touch!" (to a friend) is…
why: A negative command to one friend is non + infinitive.

q: A waiter says "Prego, si accomodi." He means…
why: si accomodi is the Lei imperative: make yourself comfortable, have a seat.

q: "I visited Rome two years ago" is…
why: A finished visit takes the passato prossimo: ho visitato.

q: "What did you do on Saturday?" (to a friend) is…
why: hai for tu, and fare has the irregular participle fatto.

q: "Ho preso" comes from which verb?
why: prendere has the irregular participle preso.

q: "I went to Florence" (a man speaking) is…
why: andare takes essere, and a man says andato.

q: "Giulia arrived yesterday" is…
why: arrivare takes essere, and the participle agrees with Giulia: arrivata.

q: Which verb takes avere in the passato prossimo?
why: mangiare takes avere; andare, partire and tornare take essere.

q: "She is very tall" is…
why: Before an adjective, molto never changes; alta agrees with lei.

q: "I have a lot of friends" is…
why: Before a noun, molto agrees: amici is masculine plural, so molti.

q: "I never drink milk" is…
why: non goes before the verb and mai after it.

q: "___ studi l'italiano? ___ mi piace." (Why…? Because…) Which word fills both blanks?
why: perché means both why and because.

q: "Me too" is…
why: Me too is anch'io; neanch'io means me neither.

q: Which is the correct spelling of "Yes, I'm coming"?
why: Yes is sì, with an accent; se means if, and si is a pronoun.

q: "Do you know Giulia?" (to a friend) is…
why: People take conoscere, and conosci is the tu form.

q: "I can swim" (I know how) is…
why: A skill takes sapere + infinitive.

q: "i parenti" means…
why: i parenti are relatives; parents are i genitori.
